title: A Nice Worksheet
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane defends the humble worksheet against what he sees as an unhelpful tendency in teaching discourse to judge activities by surface features -- whiteboards read as progressive, paper worksheets read as traditionalist -- rather than by the actual thinking students do. He describes a percent-focused worksheet he designed using Variation Theory, changing as little as possible between consecutive problems so students could carry their thinking from one item to the next, which produced strong classroom conversations about the commutativity of percents and about scaling percentages proportionally into unfamiliar ranges like 1,000%. Kane contrasts this with the double-number-line activity from his curriculum that preceded it in the same lesson: a harder, more valuable thinking task that nonetheless left several discouraged students only grudgingly participating, in visible contrast to how quickly and confidently they engaged once he switched to the worksheet. He draws two conclusions: worksheets are not inherently a problem -- they become one only when overused as repetitive drills or as a teacher's sole tool -- and different classroom activities serve different cognitive-energy needs, with a well-designed worksheet offering a legitimate, confidence-building change of pace after mentally taxing work rather than an inferior substitute for it.
points: Kane's percent worksheet used Variation Theory -- changing as little as possible between consecutive problems -- to generate classroom conversations about commutativity (30% of 50 equals 50% of 30) and proportional scaling into unfamiliar ranges like 1,000%.

He documents a visible before-and-after in student engagement: discouraged, only-grudging participation on a harder double-number-line curriculum activity, followed by immediate, confident engagement once the worksheet was introduced.
Kane's core argument rejects surface-feature judgments of teaching activities (whiteboards read as progressive, worksheets as traditionalist) in favor of judging what actual thinking a task requires.

His second, related conclusion: worksheets are a legitimate tool for managing students' cognitive energy across a lesson, offering a confidence-building change of pace rather than an inherently lesser substitute for harder tasks.
quotes: Worksheets are just pieces of paper with math problems on them. The specific problems and the way they fit together can be good or bad.

If I'm giving students problems on whiteboards I'm progressive or I value student-centered learning or the whole child or something. If I'm giving students problems on paper I'm a boring old traditionalist. That's silly.
The worksheet led to some great conversations about how percents are commutative — 30% of 50 is the same as 50% of 30, etc.
Students had been kindof grudgingly working on the double number lines with a lot of prodding from me as I ran around. Suddenly they were focused and grinding on the worksheet.
Worksheets become a problem when there's too much repetition and students stop thinking, or when they're the only pedagogical tool a teacher uses.
A worksheet can be a pleasant change of pace when students are mentally tired.
